title: Gender Sensitisation at Work
tagline: See bias, know the law, step in with confidence and build a workplace where everyone can thrive: practical gender sensitisation for Pakistan.
description:
Most gender problems at work are not caused by bad people. They come from habits nobody questions: who gets the late shift, whose idea gets credited, which WhatsApp 'joke' everyone ignores, and who is quietly left off the promotion list 'for her own good'. This certification helps every employee, manager and HR professional see those habits clearly and change them.

You will learn the difference between **sex and gender**, how **stereotypes and unconscious bias** shape decisions, and how **equality and equity** work together. You will build a business case a sceptical board will believe, and design policies on **parental leave, flexible work, day-care and safe transport** that people can actually use.

The course explains **Pakistan's legal framework** in practical terms: the constitutional guarantees, the **Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010** and its **2022 amendment**, inquiry committees, the ombudsperson, and the criminal and cybercrime routes that run alongside them. Then you practise: responding to a disclosure, preserving WhatsApp evidence, stepping in as a bystander, preventing retaliation, welcoming transgender colleagues with dignity, and measuring progress with real numbers.

Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic Pakistani workplace scenarios.
audience: All staff who want to understand gender, bias and respectful behaviour at work
Line managers and supervisors who allocate work, appraise people and receive disclosures
HR and people professionals who design policies and support inquiry committees
Inquiry committee members and competent authorities under the workplace harassment law
Senior leaders and diversity champions who set targets and report progress to boards
outcomes: Distinguish sex from gender and recognise stereotypes and unconscious bias in everyday decisions
Explain equality and equity and present a carefully framed business case for gender inclusion
Describe Pakistan's constitutional provisions and the workplace harassment law, including the 2022 amendment, complaint routes and employer duties
Recognise harassment in person and online, respond well to a disclosure and intervene safely as a bystander
Design inclusive policies and meetings, and support women's progression and transgender colleagues with dignity
Measure progress using representation, promotion-rate, attrition and pay-gap data, and report it honestly

quest.name: Mission Barabari
quest.premise: You have just joined People & Culture at Saffron Line Foods, a biscuit and tea maker with its head office in Lahore, a plant in Sheikhupura and a sales office in Karachi. The engagement survey is alarming: women are leaving, and the exit interviews don't say 'marriage'. Head of People & Culture Dr Farzana Qureshi gives you ninety days to build a plan the board will back. With a sceptical COO, a plant manager who learns to speak up, a star sales manager on the edge of resigning and a young engineer facing harassment on WhatsApp, climb five stages to the Summit Boardroom.

badge.name: Barabari Champion
badge.description: Awarded to professionals who can see bias, apply Pakistan's harassment law, step in with confidence and measure real progress towards equal footing at work.

cast.name: Dr Farzana Qureshi
cast.role: Head of People & Culture, your mentor

sessions.title: Sex, Gender, Stereotypes and the Bias We Don't See
sessions.summary: Start with yourself. Learn the difference between sex and gender, how stereotypes turn into everyday decisions, the main forms of unconscious bias at work, and simple habits that interrupt bias before it shapes a hire, a promotion or a joke.
objectives: Distinguish sex from gender, gender roles and gender norms using workplace examples
Explain how descriptive and prescriptive stereotypes, benevolent sexism and the double bind affect women and men at work
Recognise common forms of unconscious bias in hiring, appraisal and promotion decisions
Use bias interrupters such as agreed criteria, the flip test and structured discussion
Choose respectful, inclusive everyday language without becoming stiff or preachy

cards.title: Day one: the survey nobody wanted to read
cards.setting: People & Culture floor, Saffron Line Foods head office, Gulberg, Lahore. 9:15 am.

lines.text: Your first morning in People & Culture. A printed report lands on your desk, with three pages flagged in purple.
Welcome. I'm Farzana Qureshi. This is our engagement survey. Women's scores dropped in every division, and seven of our last ten manager-level resignations were women.
Farzana, with respect, women leave to get married or when the children come. That's culture, not a company problem.
Then the exit interviews should say 'marriage'. Most of them say 'no growth', 'late meetings' or 'I didn't feel safe on the night shift'.
Fine. The board wants a plan in ninety days. If you can show me it's real, I'll back it.
That's our mission. I call it Mission Barabari: equal footing for everyone at Saffron Line. And you're on it.
Stage one is the Mirror Hall. Before we fix the company, we check the assumptions we all carry, me included. Ready to look in the mirror?

cards.title: Sex and gender are not the same thing

scenes.heading: Sex: the biology
scenes.narration: Sex refers to biological characteristics: chromosomes, hormones and reproductive anatomy. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are sex-linked. So is the need for a lactation room.

scenes.heading: Gender: the script society writes
scenes.narration: Gender is the set of roles, behaviours and expectations that a society attaches to being a woman or a man. Who brews the tea, who drives, who stays late. Those are scripts, not biology.

scenes.heading: Scripts change
scenes.narration: Because gender is social, it varies between cultures, between families and over time. Your grandmother's office life looked nothing like a Karachi sales team today.

scenes.heading: Roles and norms
scenes.narration: Gender roles are the tasks people are expected to do. Gender norms are the unwritten rules that reward people who follow those roles and punish those who do not.

scenes.heading: Why it matters at work
scenes.narration: Most workplace problems come from gender scripts, not biology. 'She won't want to travel' is a script. Spotting the difference is the first skill of this mission.

cards.title: Sex or gender? Side by side
cards.caption: A quick test: if it is about bodies, it is usually sex. If it is about expectations, it is gender.

items.label: Basis
items.left: Biological characteristics
items.right: Social roles, behaviours and expectations

items.label: Variation
items.left: Largely consistent across societies
items.right: Varies across cultures, families and time

items.label: Example
items.left: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.right: Expecting the woman to leave early for the school run

items.label: Workplace need
items.left: Maternity leave, a private lactation room
items.right: Fair task allocation, no assumptions about travel

cards.title: Body or script?
cards.prompt: Sort each statement: is it linked to biological sex, or is it a gender expectation that society created?

items.text: Being able to become pregnant
The junior woman in the meeting is expected to serve the tea
Men are expected to be the main earner in the family
Needing breaks to express breast milk after childbirth
Only men are rostered on night shifts
Women are assumed to be 'naturally' suited to HR roles
Growing facial hair
Boys are told not to cry when they are upset

cards.question: Which statement describes gender rather than sex?
options: Only women can breastfeed a newborn
In one generation, women in a city started working in banks and pharmacies in large numbers
Pregnancy can cause fatigue in the first trimester
Men and women have different typical hormone levels
cards.explanation: A change within one generation in which jobs women do is a change in social roles and norms, so it is gender. The other three are biological characteristics, which is sex.

cards.title: How stereotypes do their work
cards.body:
A **stereotype** is a generalisation about a group applied to an individual. Two kinds matter at work:

- **Descriptive** stereotypes say what women or men *are* like: 'women are emotional', 'men are not caring'. They make us misjudge individuals.
- **Prescriptive** stereotypes say what they *should* be like: women should be modest, men should never ask for flexible hours. People who break them are often penalised.

This creates the **double bind**: a woman who is assertive is seen as competent but 'difficult', while one who is gentle is liked but seen as less of a leader. Men face their own version when they ask for paternity leave or say they are struggling.

Watch for **benevolent sexism** too: protective-sounding choices such as 'we won't send her to the Quetta distributor, it's too tiring for her'. It sounds kind, but it quietly removes opportunities.

Stereotypes feel like common sense. That is exactly why they need checking.

cards.back: Favouring people who are like us: same university, same city, same gender, same cricket team. It makes 'culture fit' a trap.
Noticing evidence that fits what we already believe and ignoring what doesn't. One late report 'proves' a mother is less committed.
One strong positive (halo) or negative (horns) trait colours the whole judgement of a person.
Crediting a man's success to skill and a woman's to luck or help, and blaming her failures on ability rather than circumstance.
Some groups have to show the same competence repeatedly before it is accepted, while others are judged on potential.
Assuming mothers are less committed or less mobile, so they are skipped for stretch roles, travel or promotion without being asked.

cards.title: The promotion panel
cards.setting: Board room 2, head office. The quarterly talent review. Sana Mirza joins by video from Karachi for her own item, then leaves the call.

lines.text: Next: Regional Head, North, based in Islamabad. Sana Mirza beat her targets three years running.
Strong numbers. But she has a two-year-old in Karachi. She won't want to move.
And honestly, she can be a bit aggressive with the distributors. Junaid is calmer. Steady pair of hands.
Junaid closed one deal by pushing a distributor very hard last year. We called it 'drive'.
That's... a fair point. I hadn't thought of it that way.
Nobody here is a bad person. But two biases just walked into this room. Can you name them before we vote?

cards.title: How bias keeps itself alive
cards.caption: Unconscious bias is a mental shortcut. Left alone, its results seem to prove the stereotype right.

items.label: A quick judgement
items.detail: Under time pressure, the brain reaches for a shortcut instead of the evidence.

items.label: Stereotype activated
items.detail: 'Mothers don't relocate' or 'she's too aggressive' fills the gap.

items.label: Skewed decision
items.detail: She is not asked, not shortlisted or rated lower than a man with the same record.

items.label: Fewer chances
items.detail: Without stretch roles she gains less experience and visibility.

items.label: 'See, we were right'
items.detail: Fewer women at senior levels seems to confirm the original stereotype.

cards.title: Your move on the panel
cards.situation: Farzana nods at you. The panel is about to move on and shortlist Junaid alone. Sana has the stronger results; the concerns raised are that she 'won't want to move' with a young child and is 'a bit aggressive'. Nobody has asked Sana about relocating. What do you say?

choices.text: Say nothing. You are new, and the managers know their people better than you do.
choices.outcome: Junaid is shortlisted alone. Three months later Sana hears she was never considered and starts taking calls from recruiters. Silence let the maternal wall decide.

choices.text: Propose that both are shortlisted, that Sana is asked directly about relocation like any candidate, and that 'aggressive' is tested against the same behaviour standard used for Junaid.
choices.outcome: The panel agrees. Sana says she would move, with a start date after her daughter's admission. Applying one standard to both candidates removed two biases without accusing anyone.

choices.text: Argue that Sana should get the role because the company needs more women in senior posts.
choices.outcome: The point is well meant, but it shifts the debate from merit to quotas and makes Sana look like a token. Hamid digs in. The real issue, an unfair process, never gets fixed.

choices.text: Message Sana after the meeting to tell her what Bilal and Hamid said about her.
choices.outcome: Sana is hurt and angry, trust between her and her managers breaks down, and the panel's deliberations are no longer confidential. The process stays biased, and now it is personal.

cards.title: Spot the bias in the comment
cards.prompt: Match each comment overheard at Saffron Line to the bias it best shows.

pairs.right: 'Hire Usman, he's a GCU boy like me. He'll fit right in with the team.'
'Nadia hit target because her region had an easy year. Faisal hit target because he's a closer.'
'Don't put Rabia on the Dubai project. She just came back from maternity leave.'
'Let's spare the ladies the factory audit. It's dusty and the hours are long.'
'Yes, Hina ran two plant shutdowns well, but let's see her do one more before we trust her with a third.'

cards.title: Five bias interrupters
cards.caption: You cannot switch bias off, but you can design decisions so it has less room to work.

items.label: Agree criteria first
items.detail: Decide what 'good' looks like before you see any names or CVs.

items.label: Use the same questions
items.detail: Structured interviews and appraisals, scored against the criteria.

items.label: Run the flip test
items.detail: Ask: would I say or decide this if the person were a man (or a woman)?

items.label: Ask, don't assume
items.detail: Ask every candidate about mobility or hours. Never decide for them.

items.label: Check the pattern
items.detail: Review ratings and shortlists by gender to spot gaps a single decision hides.

cards.question: A manager writes in an appraisal: 'Ayesha is too emotional in client meetings.' Using the flip test, what is the best first step?
options: Remove the comment, because appraisals should never mention behaviour
Ask what specific behaviour happened, and whether the same behaviour from a male colleague would be described the same way
Accept the comment, because the manager saw the meetings and HR did not
Ask Ayesha to attend a training course on managing emotions
cards.explanation: The flip test asks whether the same behaviour from someone of another gender would be judged the same way, and it starts with concrete behaviour. Behaviour can be appraised; vague labels such as 'emotional' often carry stereotypes. Sending her to training accepts the label without checking it.

cards.title: Inclusive language, without the lecture
cards.body:
You do not need a new vocabulary, just a little care:

- Use roles, not gender: **chairperson**, **staff hours**, **salesperson**, **team**.
- Drop put-downs that use gender as an insult, such as telling a man to 'wear bangles' or saying someone runs 'like a girl'.
- Skip questions about marriage, children or 'good news' unless the person raises them.
- Comment on work, not looks or clothes.
- Address people as they prefer: name, title, 'Sahib' or 'Madam' are all fine when used for everyone equally.

If you slip, say 'sorry, let me rephrase' and move on. No drama needed.

cards.title: Mehwish's first month on the shop floor
cards.body:
Mehwish Baloch, a process engineer from NED, is the first woman engineer at the Sheikhupura biscuit plant.

- In week one, the shift supervisor sends every maintenance query to her male junior, assuming he is the engineer.
- Bilal, meaning well, keeps her off the night shift 'for her safety', so she misses the line trials that count for confirmation.
- In meetings, her idea to cut oven downtime is ignored, then praised when a male colleague repeats it.

None of this was malicious. Each choice followed a gender script. Together they told Mehwish she did not belong.

The fix was simple once named: Bilal asked Mehwish what she needed for night shifts (safe transport and a working women's washroom), introduced her clearly as the engineer, and started crediting ideas by name in the meeting minutes.

cards.question: Bilal kept Mehwish off night shifts 'for her safety' without asking her, and she missed line trials that count for confirmation. Which concept best describes this?
options: Affinity bias
Hostile sexism
Benevolent sexism
Confirmation bias
cards.explanation: A protective-sounding decision that removes an opportunity is benevolent sexism. It is not hostile in tone, which is why it is easy to miss. The right approach is to ask her and solve the real safety issue, such as transport.

cards.title: Mirror Hall cleared
items: Sex is biological; gender is the social script of roles, behaviours and expectations, and it changes across cultures and time.
Descriptive stereotypes misjudge individuals; prescriptive ones punish people who break the script, creating the double bind.
Benevolent sexism sounds protective but removes opportunities; ask, don't assume.
Affinity, confirmation, attribution, halo/horns, prove-it-again and the maternal wall all shape hiring and promotion.
Interrupt bias with agreed criteria, structured questions, the flip test and a look at the pattern across decisions.
Inclusive language is about roles not gender, work not looks, and no gender-based insults.

cards.prompt: Think of a recent decision you made about a colleague: an assignment, a rating, a late-night task. Run the flip test on it. Would you have decided the same way if the person were of another gender? What would you check next time?

quiz.question: Which of these is the best description of 'gender' as used in workplace training?
options: The biological characteristics, such as chromosomes and hormones, that distinguish women and men
The roles, behaviours and expectations a society attaches to being a woman or a man
The sex recorded on a person's CNIC at the time it was issued
A legal category that decides which labour laws apply to an employee
quiz.explanation: Gender is social: the roles, behaviours and expectations attached to being a woman or a man, and it varies across cultures and time. Biological characteristics describe sex, not gender.

quiz.question: A plant installs a private lactation room and also stops automatically assigning meeting minutes to the youngest woman present. Which statement is correct?
options: The lactation room responds to a sex-linked need; the minutes change addresses a gender expectation
Both changes respond to biological sex differences
Both changes address gender expectations only
The lactation room addresses a gender expectation; the minutes change responds to a sex-linked need
quiz.explanation: Breastfeeding is biological, so the lactation room responds to a sex-linked need. Who takes the minutes is a social expectation, so changing that addresses gender.

quiz.question: 'Women should be modest and not push for a raise.' What kind of stereotype is this?
options: A descriptive stereotype, because it describes how women typically behave
Affinity bias, because it favours people similar to the speaker
A prescriptive stereotype, because it says how women ought to behave
A sex-linked fact, because it reflects a biological difference
quiz.explanation: Prescriptive stereotypes say how a group should behave and penalise people who break the script. Descriptive stereotypes claim to describe how a group is.

quiz.question: A female manager who gives direct feedback is called 'harsh', while her male peer doing the same is called 'decisive'. If she softens her style, she is called 'not leadership material'. What is this pattern called?
options: The halo effect
Confirmation bias
The maternal wall
The double bind
quiz.explanation: The double bind means a woman is penalised either way: assertive and seen as unlikeable, or warm and seen as less competent. The halo effect is one trait colouring the whole judgement.

quiz.question: A sales director decides not to send the only woman on his team to a three-day distributor conference in Quetta because 'the travel would be too tiring for her'. She was not asked. What is the best description?
options: Reasonable care, because a manager is responsible for staff welfare on travel
Benevolent sexism that removes an opportunity without asking her
Hostile sexism, because the manager dislikes women in sales
Affinity bias, because he prefers to travel with men
quiz.explanation: The decision sounds protective but takes away a development opportunity on the basis of gender, without her input. That is benevolent sexism. Real welfare care means asking her and addressing any genuine travel or safety needs.

quiz.question: A hiring manager says, 'Let's take Hassan; he went to my university and played in the same cricket league, so he'll fit in.' Which bias is most clearly at work?
options: Attribution bias
Prove-it-again bias
Affinity bias
Benevolent sexism
quiz.explanation: Affinity bias is favouring people similar to ourselves. 'Fit' based on shared background is a common way it enters hiring.

quiz.question: Two officers both exceed target. The appraisal says the man 'drove results through strong negotiation', while the woman 'benefited from a favourable territory'. Which bias does this most clearly show?
options: Attribution bias
Affinity bias
Halo effect
Maternal wall
quiz.explanation: Attribution bias credits one group's success to skill and another's to luck or circumstances. The same result has been explained differently by gender.

quiz.question: What does the 'flip test' ask a decision-maker to do?
options: Reverse the order in which candidates are interviewed to avoid fatigue
Ask a colleague of the other gender to review the decision and make the final call in your place
Give the candidate a chance to reply to any negative comment
Check whether the same decision or comment would be made if the person were of another gender
quiz.explanation: The flip test swaps the gender in your mind and asks whether you would still say or decide the same thing. It is a quick way to surface a stereotype.

quiz.question: Which change to a promotion process most directly reduces the chance that bias shapes the result?
options: Letting each panel member use their own judgement of 'leadership presence'
Agreeing the criteria before reviewing candidates and scoring everyone against them
Asking line managers to nominate the people they feel most comfortable with
Deciding in a quick meeting so people rely on their first impressions
quiz.explanation: Criteria agreed in advance and applied to everyone leave less room for shortcuts and stereotypes. Vague 'presence', comfort and first impressions are exactly where bias operates.

quiz.question: In a team meeting a manager says to a male officer who missed a target, 'Come on, stop acting like a girl and wear bangles if you can't handle it.' What is the best view?
options: It's harmless banter that men in sales teams are used to, and it was aimed at a man, not at women
It is only a problem if a woman is present in the meeting
It is inappropriate, because it uses gender as an insult and demeans women and the officer
It is fine if the officer laughs along at the time
quiz.explanation: Using femininity as an insult demeans women and shames the man for not fitting a gender script. Whether women are present or the target laughs does not make it acceptable.

sessions.title: Equality, Equity and the Case for Change
sessions.summary: Build a case the board will believe. Separate equality from equity, use well-established evidence without overclaiming, anchor the case in Pakistan's Constitution, and design practical policies on leave, flexible work, day-care and safe transport that actually get used.
objectives: Explain the difference between equality and equity and why equity measures are not favours
Present a business case for gender inclusion using carefully framed evidence
Identify the constitutional provisions on equality, non-discrimination and women's participation
Design inclusive policies on parental leave, flexible work, day-care and safe transport
Distinguish a policy that exists on paper from one that people can use without penalty

cards.title: Show me the numbers
cards.setting: COO's office, head office, Lahore. Rain on the window, chai going cold.

lines.text: I read your Mirror Hall notes. Fair points. But I run a profit and loss account, not a debating society. Why should Saffron Line spend money on this?
Because we are paying already. Every manager who resigns costs us recruitment, training and lost sales. We just don't see it on one line.
(on speaker from Karachi) And I'm not asking for less work, Hamid sahib. I'm asking for a different shape of work. Two days from home would keep me.
At the plant, Mehwish's problem is simpler. The last staff bus leaves at 7 pm on an unlit road. The night line trials end at 10.
So we treat everyone the same and let them sort out their own transport. That's equality, isn't it?
Same treatment for people starting from different places doesn't give the same chance. Welcome to the Ledger Room. Let's balance the books properly.

scenes.heading: Equality: the same for everyone
scenes.narration: Equality means treating everyone the same: the same rules, the same bus, the same leave. It is a good starting point and it is the goal for rights and pay for equal work.

scenes.heading: When 'the same' isn't fair
scenes.narration: But people start from different places. One staff bus at 7 pm treats everyone equally, yet only the engineer who cannot safely walk an unlit road at 10 pm loses the chance to attend trials.

scenes.heading: Equity: fair treatment for different needs
scenes.narration: Equity means adjusting support so that everyone has a genuinely fair chance. A late-shift drop service for anyone on night trials is an equity measure.

scenes.heading: Equity serves equality
scenes.narration: Equity is the route, equality of opportunity is the destination. Equity measures are not favours or lower standards. Everyone still meets the same bar.

scenes.heading: Our Constitution agrees
scenes.narration: Pakistan's Constitution forbids discrimination on the basis of sex alone, and it also allows special provision for the protection of women. Equality and equity sit side by side.

cards.title: Equality or equity in practice
cards.caption: Both have a place. Equity closes the gap so that equal rules become fair in reality.

items.label: Transport
items.left: One staff bus at 7 pm for all
items.right: Drop service for anyone on late shifts

items.label: Promotion
items.left: Same criteria for all candidates
items.right: Same criteria, plus sponsorship for groups who lack networks

items.label: Facilities
items.left: One shared washroom block
items.right: Separate, safe, lockable facilities for women

items.label: Standard
items.left: Same bar for everyone
items.right: Same bar for everyone: support changes, standards don't

cards.question: A pharma company offers a late-evening drop service to every employee whose field visits end after 8 pm, after women reps said they were turning down evening doctor meetings. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is a favour for women that lowers standards for men
It breaks the principle of equality, because some staff get a service others don't
It is an equity measure that removes a barrier so everyone can meet the same targets
It is only needed if the law specifically requires it
cards.explanation: Equity adjusts support to remove barriers so everyone has a fair chance to meet the same standard. The targets are unchanged and the service is available to anyone working late, so no standard is lowered.

cards.title: The context in four numbers
cards.caption: Use well-established figures, say where they come from in general terms, and check the latest edition before you present them.

items.label: Women in Pakistan's labour force
items.detail: Recent labour force surveys and international estimates put women's participation far below men's. Check the latest survey.

items.label: Global gender gap ranking
items.detail: Pakistan has ranked among the lowest countries in a widely cited international gender gap index in recent editions.

items.label: Diverse leadership teams
items.detail: Large global consultancy studies link gender-diverse executive teams to above-average profitability. A link, not proof of cause.

items.label: Share of the population
items.detail: Women are nearly half of Pakistan's people, and so nearly half of potential customers, patients and account holders.

cards.title: A business case that survives the boardroom
cards.body:
Five strands a sceptical board will accept:

- **Talent**: hiring from only half the population shrinks the pool. Graduates are increasingly women in many fields.
- **Retention cost**: replacing a manager means recruitment fees, months of ramp-up and lost relationships. Calculate it from your own data.
- **Customers**: women influence household spending, health choices and savings. Teams that reflect customers design better products.
- **Decisions**: varied teams challenge groupthink and spot risks earlier.
- **Risk and law**: harassment and discrimination bring legal, regulatory and reputational damage.

Frame evidence honestly. Studies showing that diverse firms do better show a **correlation**, not proof that diversity alone *causes* profit. Say so; boards trust presenters who don't overclaim.

And keep the **rights case** beside the business case: fair treatment is required by law and values even when it does not pay off in a quarter.

cards.title: Solid claim or overclaim?
cards.prompt: Farzana is checking slides for the board. Sort each statement: is it a solid, defensible claim, or an overclaim she should rewrite?

items.text: Gender diversity guarantees higher profits
Global studies link gender-diverse leadership teams with above-average profitability
Our exit data show 7 of the last 10 manager resignations were women
Hiring one woman manager will raise our sales by 20%
Replacing a manager costs us recruitment fees and months of lost productivity, based on last year's cases
Every company that ignores gender will fail within five years
Women's labour force participation in Pakistan is far below men's, according to recent surveys

cards.title: Where equality rules come from
cards.caption: Higher layers set the frame; the lower layers decide what people actually experience on a Tuesday afternoon.

items.label: The Constitution
items.detail: Equality before law, no discrimination on the basis of sex alone, women's full participation.

items.label: Federal and provincial laws
items.detail: Harassment, labour, maternity, transgender rights and cybercrime laws.

items.label: Regulators' policies
items.detail: Sector rules and guidance, for example the banking regulator's gender policy.

items.label: Company policy
items.detail: Code of conduct, leave, flexible work, transport and grievance procedures.

items.label: Daily practice
items.detail: What managers actually approve, say and tolerate.

cards.title: The Constitution on your side
cards.prompt: Match each constitutional provision to what it broadly says. (Wording is paraphrased; read the text itself for exact language.)

pairs.right: Citizens are equal before law; no discrimination on the basis of sex alone; the State may make special provision for women and children
No discrimination on grounds including sex in appointments to the service of Pakistan, for a qualified citizen
Steps to be taken to ensure women's full participation in all spheres of national life
Just and humane conditions of work, including maternity benefits for women in employment

cards.title: Policies on paper
cards.setting: Video call: Lahore, Karachi and the Sheikhupura plant. Farzana shares the HR policy manual on screen.

lines.text: Good news: we already have a flexible work policy. Bad news: in three years, only two people have used it.
Because the last person who asked was told she 'wasn't serious about her career'. Everyone heard about it.
Same at the plant. We have paternity leave, three days. No man has taken it. They'd be teased for a month.
And the policy says 'transport on request'. But I have to ask my shift supervisor every single time, and he sighs.
So a policy isn't real until people can use it without paying a price. Let's design them properly.

cards.back: Paid leave around childbirth, required by labour laws. Good practice adds job protection, a phased return and no penalty on appraisal for the leave period.
Paid leave for fathers. Some recent Pakistani laws provide it; check yours. When men actually take it, care stops being seen as 'women's work'.
Options such as remote days, staggered hours or compressed weeks, open to all roles where the work allows, judged on output.
On-site crèche, a partner centre or an allowance. Some older factory laws already require a room for young children where many women work.
A private, clean, lockable room (not a washroom) with a fridge and break time for mothers returning from leave.
Pick-and-drop for late or early shifts, verified drivers, safe routes and a rule about who is dropped last.
A planned re-entry after leave or a career break: keep-in-touch days, a buddy, refresher training and a clear role.

cards.title: Sana's request
cards.situation: Sana formally requests to work from home on Mondays and Fridays for six months while her daughter settles into school. Her role is mostly calls, reports and distributor reviews; she visits the market Tuesday to Thursday. Her line manager, Junaid, forwards the request to you with the note: 'If I say yes, everyone will want it.' How do you advise him?

choices.text: Decline it; making exceptions creates unfairness and Sana can resign if it doesn't suit her.
choices.outcome: Sana resigns two months later and joins a competitor with her distributor relationships. Replacing her takes five months. 'No exceptions' cost far more than the flexibility would have.

choices.text: Approve it quietly as a personal favour, and ask Sana not to tell anyone.
choices.outcome: Sana stays, but colleagues notice and resent the 'secret deal'. The next request is refused by a different manager. A hidden favour creates exactly the unfairness Junaid feared.

choices.text: Assess it against the role's needs and the policy, agree output measures and a review date, and apply the same approach to any future request from anyone.
choices.outcome: Junaid approves a six-month trial with clear targets. Sana's numbers hold. Two other staff, including a man caring for his father, apply under the same rules. Fair, visible and manageable.

cards.title: Designing a safe transport policy
cards.prompt: Bilal wants a late-shift transport policy for the plant that people will actually trust. Put the steps in the best order.
steps: Map the risk: shift end times, routes, lighting and where staff live
Consult the people affected, including women on late shifts, in a safe setting
Design the service: pick-and-drop, verified drivers, safe drop order and an emergency contact
Write it into policy so it applies automatically, with no per-trip permission needed
Communicate it to all staff and supervisors
Monitor use, incidents and feedback, then adjust

cards.title: Leave and care: know your current law
cards.body:
Pakistan's leave rules sit in several laws and have changed recently, so always **check the version that applies to your organisation and province**.

- **Maternity benefits** have long been required by labour law for women employees, with paid leave around childbirth and protection from dismissal during it. Since the 18th Amendment, labour is largely a provincial subject, so provinces have their own versions.
- **Paternity leave** is newer. Recent federal legislation for Islamabad extended maternity leave and introduced paid paternity leave, and some provinces have moved in the same direction.
- **Sector rules** add more. The banking regulator's gender policy, for example, set targets for women's representation and encouraged measures such as day-care.

Good employers treat the law as the floor. They make leave **gender-neutral where possible** (so mothers don't become the 'expensive' hire), protect appraisals during leave and plan the return.

cards.question: Saffron Line already offers three days' paternity leave, but no man has taken it in three years. What is the most likely issue and fix?
options: Men don't need leave, so the policy should be withdrawn
The leave is too long and should be cut to one day
The problem is legal, so the company should wait for a new law
A gender norm makes using it costly; senior men taking it visibly and managers endorsing it would help
cards.explanation: A policy that exists but is never used usually has a cultural cost attached. Visible role models and managers who endorse it remove the stigma. Withdrawing or shortening it would reinforce the idea that care is women's work.

cards.title: The Karachi flexible-work pilot
cards.body:
After Sana's trial, Farzana ran a six-month pilot across the Karachi sales office.

- **Rules**: any role could apply; managers judged requests on the job's needs, agreed output targets and set a review date.
- **Uptake**: 14 of 38 staff applied, 6 of them men. Requests included school runs, an MBA and caring for a parent.
- **Results**: sales targets were met, and voluntary resignations fell compared with the same period last year. Farzana reported this as encouraging, not as proof, since the market also improved.
- **Lesson**: open to everyone, visible rules and output measures made flexibility normal rather than a 'mothers' favour'.

Hamid read the one-page summary twice. 'Fine,' he said. 'Now do the plant.'

cards.title: Ledger Room balanced
items: Equality is the same treatment; equity adjusts support to remove barriers so everyone can meet the same standard.
A credible business case uses talent, retention cost, customers, decision quality and risk, and presents studies as correlations, not guarantees.
The Constitution forbids discrimination on the basis of sex alone (Article 25), allows special provision for women, and calls for women's full participation (Article 34).
Inclusive policies cover parental leave, flexible work, day-care, lactation rooms, safe transport and return-to-work support.
A policy is real only when people can use it without a career penalty; gender-neutral design helps.
Leave and care laws differ by province and have changed recently: always check the current version.

cards.prompt: Pick one policy in your organisation that exists on paper. Who actually uses it, and who doesn't? What unwritten cost might be stopping people, and what one change would make it genuinely usable?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes equity in a workplace setting?
options: Giving every employee exactly the same resources and rules, regardless of their individual circumstances
Setting lower performance standards for groups that have faced barriers
Adjusting support so people facing different barriers have a fair chance to meet the same standard
Hiring equal numbers of women and men in every department
quiz.explanation: Equity adjusts support, not standards, so that everyone has a genuinely fair chance. Identical resources is equality; lowering standards or rigid number-matching is neither.

quiz.question: A bank's only staff van leaves the regional office at 6 pm. Women officers decline month-end late duties that are counted in promotion decisions. Which response is an equity measure?
options: Remove month-end duties from the promotion criteria for women only
Keep the van at 6 pm because it is the same for everyone
Ask women officers to arrange their own transport if they want promotion
Provide a late drop for anyone working month-end duties
quiz.explanation: A late drop for anyone on late duties removes the barrier while keeping the same promotion criteria for all. Changing the criteria for women only lowers the standard rather than removing the barrier.

quiz.question: A consultant tells your board: 'Studies prove that adding women to the executive team will increase your profits.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: Studies link gender-diverse leadership with above-average profitability, but a link is not proof of cause
Studies show diversity has no relationship with company performance
The claim is correct, is backed by every major global study, and should be presented to the board as a guarantee
No research exists on this topic, so it should not be mentioned
quiz.explanation: The research shows a correlation. Presenting it as proof of cause overclaims and undermines trust. Saying no research exists or no link exists is also wrong.

quiz.question: Which constitutional provision expressly allows the State to make special provision for the protection of women, alongside forbidding discrimination on the basis of sex alone?
options: Article 34
Article 25
Article 37(e)
Article 27
quiz.explanation: Article 25 sets equality before law, forbids discrimination on the basis of sex alone and permits special provision for women and children. Article 34 concerns women's full participation in national life.

quiz.question: Which constitutional provision refers to just and humane conditions of work and maternity benefits for women in employment?
options: Article 25
Article 27
Article 34
Article 37(e)
quiz.explanation: Article 37(e), a principle of policy, refers to just and humane conditions of work and maternity benefits for women in employment.

quiz.question: A company has a flexible work policy, but it has been used twice in three years and staff say requesters are seen as 'not serious'. What does this best show?
options: A policy is not real until people can use it without a career penalty
Staff do not want flexibility, so the policy can be withdrawn
The policy should be restricted to women so it is used more
Flexible work only suits head-office roles
quiz.explanation: Low use plus reported stigma means the policy has a hidden cost. Restricting it to women would deepen the stigma; the fix is visible, fair rules and manager support.

quiz.question: Why do many employers make parental leave and flexible work policies gender-neutral?
options: Because the law always requires identical leave for mothers and fathers
Because women do not need maternity-specific provisions
So care is shared and women are not seen as the only 'costly' hires
So the company can reduce maternity leave to match paternity leave
quiz.explanation: Gender-neutral design shares care between parents and reduces the perception that hiring women is more costly. Maternity-specific needs such as recovery and breastfeeding still remain.

quiz.question: An HR officer in Peshawar wants to confirm how many weeks of paid maternity leave her company must provide. What is the best approach?
options: Use the figure from a training slide from several years ago
Check the current law for her organisation and province, including recent amendments
Apply the Islamabad federal rule, since federal labour law applies equally in every province
Copy the policy of a competitor in Lahore
quiz.explanation: Labour matters are largely provincial since the 18th Amendment, and leave laws have changed recently. She must check the current law that applies to her organisation and location.

quiz.question: Which room setup meets good practice for mothers returning from maternity leave?
options: A private, clean, lockable room that is not a washroom, with a fridge and agreed break time
A spare cubicle in the women's washroom
The prayer room, between prayer times
A corner of the canteen with a screen
quiz.explanation: A lactation room should be private, hygienic, lockable and not a washroom, with refrigeration and protected break time. Shared or public spaces fail on privacy and hygiene.

quiz.question: When designing a late-shift transport policy, which step should come before designing the service itself?
options: Communicating the new policy to all supervisors
Monitoring incidents and feedback
Writing the service into the HR manual
Consulting the people affected, including women on late shifts
quiz.explanation: Map the risk and consult those affected first, then design, write into policy, communicate and monitor. Designing without consultation often misses the real problem.

sessions.title: Pakistan's Harassment Law: What It Says and How It Works
sessions.summary: Know the rules before you need them. Learn what the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010 requires, how the 2022 amendment broadened it, how the inquiry committee and the ombudsperson work, and how criminal and cybercrime laws sit alongside it.
objectives: Explain what the 2010 workplace harassment Act defines as harassment and how the 2022 amendment broadened its scope
List an employer's core duties: the code of conduct, its display and the inquiry committee
Describe the two complaint routes, the inquiry steps and their broad timelines, and the appeal route
Distinguish minor and major penalties and explain how false complaints are treated
Recognise when criminal and cybercrime laws may also apply, and why the current text must always be checked

cards.title: The screenshots
cards.setting: Farzana's office, head office, Lahore. 8:40 pm. A WhatsApp call from the Sheikhupura plant.

lines.text: I'm sorry to call so late. I've sent you screenshots. Kashif, my shift supervisor, messages me after midnight. 'You looked beautiful today.' 'Why don't you reply?' I've asked him to stop. Twice.
And today someone in the 'Shift B' group posted an edited photo of me. Twenty-six people saw it. Some laughed.
Thank you for telling me, Mehwish. You did the right thing, and you're not in trouble. Please keep every screenshot.
(joining the call) Farzana, I'll have a word with Kashif. But the group is on personal phones, not at work. Is that even our business?
It's very much our business, Bilal, and 'a word' isn't the process. There's a law, a code and a committee for exactly this.
Stage three is the Code Wall. Let's learn exactly what the law says, so that Mehwish gets a fair process and so does Kashif.

scenes.heading: A law for every workplace
scenes.narration: In 2010 Pakistan passed the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act. It applies to public and private organisations, and it gives employees a clear way to complain and be heard.

scenes.heading: What harassment means
scenes.narration: The Act covers unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favours and other verbal, written or physical conduct of a sexual nature, or sexually demeaning attitudes, that interfere with work or create an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment.

scenes.heading: Including 'do this or else'
scenes.narration: It also covers making a job, promotion or benefit depend on going along, and punishing someone for refusing. Despite its title, the Act lets a man complain too.

scenes.heading: The employer's duties
scenes.narration: Every organisation must adopt the code of conduct set out in the Act as part of its policy, display it prominently, and set up an inquiry committee to hear complaints.

scenes.heading: 2022: a wider net
scenes.narration: An amendment in 2022 broadened the Act. Harassment now also covers discrimination on the basis of gender, and the meanings of employee and workplace were widened. Always read the current text.

cards.title: Milestones in the legal framework
cards.caption: Several laws work together. Dates are the years the laws were made; check the current versions and any provincial laws.

items.label: The Constitution
items.detail: Equality before law, no discrimination on the basis of sex alone, women's full participation.

items.label: Workplace harassment Act
items.detail: Code of conduct, inquiry committees and the ombudsperson.

items.label: Penal Code amendment
items.detail: Sexual harassment made a specific criminal offence alongside the workplace Act.

items.label: Electronic crimes law (PECA)
items.detail: Online offences such as cyberstalking and misuse of intimate images.

items.label: Transgender persons law
items.detail: Includes protection against discrimination at work. Parts were later challenged in court.

items.label: Harassment Act amendment
items.detail: Broader meanings of harassment, employee and workplace, including gender discrimination.

cards.back: The person who makes the complaint of harassment. Under the Act this has never been limited to women.
The employee against whom the complaint is made. The accused has a right to know the charges and to defend themselves.
The organisation's own three-member committee that hears complaints, with at least one woman member.
The official the organisation designates to act on the committee's findings and impose any penalty.
An independent office, federal or provincial, that can hear complaints directly and hear appeals against an organisation's decision.
The standards of behaviour set out in the Act. Organisations must adopt it as policy and display it prominently.

cards.title: What the 2022 amendment changed (in general terms)
cards.body:
The 2022 amendment answered criticism that the original Act was too narrow. In broad terms it:

- **Widened 'harassment'** so that it is no longer limited to conduct of a sexual nature: **discrimination on the basis of gender** (for example, being sidelined or denied opportunities because of gender) is included.
- **Widened 'employee'** to cover more working people beyond permanent staff, such as contract, temporary and some unpaid or non-traditional workers.
- **Widened 'workplace'** beyond the office building to places where work-related activity happens.

In practice, this means work trips, client sites, events and work-related messaging groups are not a 'grey zone'.

**Caution:** the precise definitions and lists are in the amended text, and provinces have their own versions. Always read the current law, or ask your legal team, before relying on a specific detail.

cards.title: Within the Act's definition?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation at Saffron Line: likely to fall within the Act's (amended) definition of harassment, or not harassment as such, though it may need another response.

items.text: A supervisor keeps sending late-night personal messages after being asked to stop
An edited photo of a colleague is posted in a work WhatsApp group
A manager gives fair, specific feedback on missed delivery targets
Confirmation is made conditional on agreeing to 'private dinners'
A colleague invites a co-worker to a team lunch once, accepts 'no' and never asks again
A woman engineer is deliberately kept off all site work because 'women don't belong on the floor'
Two colleagues disagree loudly about a budget, with no personal or gendered remarks
Repeated sexual jokes are aimed at a colleague who has shown they are unwelcome

cards.title: The employer's core duties
cards.caption: These are the basics every organisation must have in place, whatever its size. Check the current law for details.

items.label: Adopt the code
items.detail: Make the Act's code of conduct part of HR and management policy.

items.label: Display it
items.detail: Post it prominently in English and in a language most staff understand (usually Urdu), where everyone can see it.

items.label: Form the committee
items.detail: Three members, at least one a woman, usually including senior management and an employees' representative.

items.label: Designate the authority
items.detail: Name the competent authority who acts on findings.

items.label: Make it work
items.detail: Train members, publicise how to complain, keep records and protect people from retaliation.

cards.question: Saffron Line's plant forms an inquiry committee of three senior male managers 'because they are the most experienced'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as they are senior
The committee must have exactly two women
At least one member of the three-member committee must be a woman
Inquiry committees must be made up of outside lawyers
cards.explanation: The Act requires a three-member committee with at least one woman. Seniority is useful but cannot replace that requirement. External members are not mandatory.

cards.title: Two doors
cards.setting: Plant meeting room, Sheikhupura. Bilal and Farzana, with the code of conduct pinned to the wall behind them.

lines.text: I've read the code. So Mehwish has to complain to our committee? Kashif's uncle sits on it.
Then he must step aside from this case. And she has a choice of doors: our inquiry committee, or straight to the ombudsperson.
And if she goes inside and doesn't like the outcome? Or if Kashif thinks it's unfair?
Either side can appeal to the ombudsperson. That's why the process must be clean from day one: written charges, a chance to defend, evidence, records.
And if it turns out to be false?
The law deals with deliberately false complaints too. But a complaint that can't be proved is not the same as a false one. Let's walk through it.

cards.title: Two routes for a complaint
cards.caption: The complainant chooses. A criminal or cybercrime complaint can also be made separately where the conduct may be an offence.

items.label: Who runs it
items.left: The organisation's own three-member committee
items.right: An independent federal or provincial office

items.label: When used
items.left: Complainant chooses to raise it inside
items.right: Complainant goes directly, or either side appeals

items.label: Outcome
items.left: Findings to the competent authority, who imposes any penalty
items.right: Its own decision on the complaint or appeal

items.label: Best for
items.left: Quick, local resolution where trust exists
items.right: Independence, e.g. when the accused is senior or close to the committee

cards.title: The inquiry, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the stages of an inquiry committee case in order. (The Act sets short time limits for several steps; check the current text.)
steps: A written complaint reaches the inquiry committee
Within a few days, the accused is given the charges and allegations in writing
The accused submits a written defence, within about a week
The committee hears both sides and examines evidence and witnesses
The committee sends its findings and recommendations to the competent authority, within about a month of starting
The competent authority decides and imposes any penalty, within about a week
Either party may appeal to the ombudsperson within the appeal period

cards.title: Outcomes the law provides for
cards.prompt: Match each term to what it covers under the Act (paraphrased).

pairs.right: Censure, withholding a promotion or increment for a period, or recovering compensation for the complainant from the accused's pay
Demotion, compulsory retirement, removal or dismissal from service, or a fine
Where a complaint is found to be made falsely with bad intent, action can be recommended against the complainant
A party unhappy with the competent authority's decision can take it to the ombudsperson within the set period
An organisation that fails to meet its duties, such as forming a committee, can be fined

cards.title: Mehwish asks what to do
cards.situation: Mehwish meets you at head office. She is anxious: 'I want it to stop. I don't want to ruin his life, but I don't want to be the one who leaves. And his uncle is on the committee.' She asks what her options are. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell her the internal committee is the only route and she must file there today, or the company can't help.
choices.outcome: Mehwish feels cornered, given the uncle's seat. She delays, and the messages continue. Pushing a single route ignores her choice and the conflict of interest.

choices.text: Explain her options plainly: informal resolution, a formal complaint to the committee (the uncle stepping aside) or the ombudsperson directly; confidentiality; no retaliation; interim steps. Let her choose.
choices.outcome: Mehwish chooses a formal complaint to the committee once you confirm the uncle will recuse himself. She feels in control. The case starts fairly for both sides.

choices.text: Suggest she first talks to Kashif herself and tells him firmly to stop.
choices.outcome: She has already done this twice. Asking her to confront him again puts the burden on her. Direct communication can be one informal option if she wants it, but not the advice by itself.

choices.text: Call Kashif in yourself, warn him off and close the matter without a record.
choices.outcome: Kashif guesses who complained and the messages stop, but the group members turn cold on Mehwish. No record, no process, no protection. If it happens again, there is nothing on file.

cards.title: Other laws that may apply
cards.body:
The workplace Act is not the only law. The same conduct may also be:

- **A criminal offence under the Pakistan Penal Code.** Since 2010 the Penal Code has specifically covered sexual harassment. A criminal complaint goes to the police and courts, not to the inquiry committee.
- **A cybercrime under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA)**, for example cyberstalking, or sharing someone's intimate or edited images to harm them. Complaints go to the federal cybercrime investigation agency; this function has moved between agencies in recent years, so check the current reporting channel.
- **Discrimination under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018**, which includes protection at work.

These routes can run **alongside** the workplace route. Provinces have also passed their own harassment laws and ombudspersons, so which office applies depends on where and how the organisation operates. Check, and take legal advice for serious cases.

cards.question: Bilal says the 'Shift B' WhatsApp group isn't covered because it is on personal phones. What is the best answer?
options: He is right; only conduct inside the plant building counts
It is covered only if the company pays for the phones
It can only be dealt with by the police, not the company
Work-related messaging among colleagues can fall within the workplace process, and PECA may also apply to edited images
cards.explanation: The 2022 amendment widened the idea of workplace beyond the building, and a group of colleagues organised around shifts is work-related. Sharing an edited image may also be a cybercrime. The company process and criminal routes can run in parallel.

cards.title: Check the current law, every time
cards.body:
Time limits, definitions and penalties in this stage are summarised from the Act as it is generally understood, and amendments, provincial laws and court rulings change the details.

- Keep a copy of the **current** Act and any provincial version on file.
- Ask your legal team which ombudsperson (federal or provincial) applies to your organisation.
- Write time limits into your procedure and track them in a case log.
- When in doubt, get advice before a deadline passes, not after.

cards.title: Code Wall scaled
items: The 2010 Act covers sexual advances, requests for favours, sexual conduct or demeaning attitudes that interfere with work, plus 'comply or else' pressure; men can complain too.
The 2022 amendment broadened harassment to include gender discrimination and widened 'employee' and 'workplace'.
Employers must adopt and prominently display the code, form a three-member inquiry committee with at least one woman, and name a competent authority.
Complainants can go to the inquiry committee or directly to the ombudsperson; decisions can be appealed to the ombudsperson.
Inquiries run on short time limits; penalties are minor or major; deliberately false complaints can lead to action.
Criminal and cybercrime routes can run in parallel. Always check the current text and the provincial position.

cards.prompt: Do you know who sits on your organisation's inquiry committee, and where the code of conduct is displayed? If someone came to you tomorrow, could you explain both complaint routes in two minutes? Write down what you would need to find out.

quiz.question: Under the 2010 Act, how must an organisation's inquiry committee be made up?
options: Three members, at least one of whom is a woman
Five members, all from senior management
Two members: one from HR and one external lawyer
Any number of members, as long as the chair is a woman
quiz.explanation: The Act requires a three-member inquiry committee with at least one woman member.

quiz.question: Which statement about who can complain under the 2010 Act is correct?
options: Only women employees can complain, as the title says
Only permanent employees with at least one year's service can complain
A man can also make a complaint under the Act
Only people who have already reported to the police can complain
quiz.explanation: Despite its title, the Act's complainant has never been limited to women; a man can also complain. There is no length-of-service or police-report requirement.

quiz.question: In broad terms, what did the 2022 amendment do to the meaning of harassment?
options: It limited harassment to physical conduct only
It broadened it to include discrimination on the basis of gender, not just sexual conduct
It removed 'requests for sexual favours' from the definition
It restricted complaints to incidents that take place inside the employer's own office buildings
quiz.explanation: The 2022 amendment widened the definition so it is not limited to sexual conduct and includes discrimination on the basis of gender. It also widened 'employee' and 'workplace'.

quiz.question: What must an organisation do with the code of conduct under the Act?
options: Keep it confidential in the HR department
Send it only to the inquiry committee
Publish it online only
Adopt it as part of its policy and display it prominently in languages staff understand
quiz.explanation: The code must be adopted as part of the organisation's policy and displayed prominently, in English and in a language most staff understand (usually Urdu), so everyone knows the standard and how to complain.

quiz.question: A clerk in a private firm in Islamabad does not trust her internal committee because the accused is her director. What option does the Act give her?
options: None; she must use the internal committee first
She may only resign and then sue for damages
She can complain directly to the ombudsperson
She must ask the director's permission to go outside
quiz.explanation: The complainant may choose to go to the inquiry committee or directly to the ombudsperson. Going directly is useful where the accused is senior or close to the committee.

quiz.question: Once a written complaint reaches the inquiry committee, what is the next step in the inquiry?
options: The competent authority immediately imposes a penalty
The accused is given the charges and allegations in writing within a few days
The complaint is sent to the police for investigation
The complainant is asked to withdraw and try informal resolution first
quiz.explanation: The accused must promptly receive the charges in writing so they can prepare a defence. Penalties come only after findings, and the police route is separate.

quiz.question: Which of these is a major penalty under the Act?
options: Censure
Withholding an increment for a period
Recovering compensation for the complainant from the accused's pay
Removal from service
quiz.explanation: Removal and dismissal from service, compulsory retirement, demotion and fines are major penalties. Censure, withholding increments or promotion for a period and recovery of compensation are minor penalties.

quiz.question: The committee finds there is not enough evidence to prove a complaint, but nothing suggests the complainant lied. What follows?
options: The complaint is not proved, but this does not make it a false complaint deserving action
The complainant must be penalised for a false complaint
The case automatically goes to the police
The accused must still receive at least a minor penalty, since the complaint was not withdrawn
quiz.explanation: Action against a complainant is for complaints found to be false and made with bad intent. A complaint that cannot be proved is different, and punishing it would deter genuine reports.

quiz.question: A colleague circulates an edited, sexualised image of a female co-worker in a WhatsApp group. Besides the workplace route, which law may also apply?
options: The Companies Act
The Contract Act
The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016
The Factories Act
quiz.explanation: PECA 2016 covers online offences such as cyberstalking and misusing someone's images to harm them. A cybercrime complaint can run alongside the workplace process.

quiz.question: Who imposes the penalty after an inquiry committee completes its findings?
options: The inquiry committee chair
The competent authority designated by the organisation
The complainant
The local police station
quiz.explanation: The committee sends findings and recommendations to the competent authority, who decides and imposes any penalty. Either party can then appeal to the ombudsperson.

sessions.title: Recognise, Respond, Step In: Harassment in Real Life
sessions.summary: Turn the law into action. Recognise harassment in person and on WhatsApp, respond well when someone confides in you, protect people from retaliation, step in safely as a bystander, and practise everyday allyship, especially as a man, in meetings and beyond.
objectives: Recognise the range of harassing behaviour, including online and messaging-app patterns, using impact rather than intent
Respond to a disclosure as a colleague or manager in a way that is supportive, fair and procedurally sound
Preserve evidence of online harassment correctly
Use the five Ds of bystander intervention and recognise retaliation
Practise allyship and run inclusive meetings

cards.title: The silence after
cards.setting: Plant canteen, Sheikhupura. Two weeks after Mehwish's complaint. Lunch break.

lines.text: The inquiry is under way. Kashif has been moved to a different shift while it runs. But something else is happening.
Nobody sits with me now. The Shift B group was deleted and a new one made. I wasn't added. My line data 'goes missing' before reviews.
I need to tell you something, Farzana. I was in that group. I saw the photo the day it was posted. I didn't say anything.
Thank you for saying it, Bilal. Most people stay silent because they don't know what to do, not because they agree.
But what's happening to Mehwish now has a name: retaliation. And silence from twenty-six people helped it start.
Stage four is the Bystander Bridge. Let's learn to see it early, respond well and step in, without making things worse.

scenes.heading: The question is how it lands
scenes.narration: Harassment is judged by whether conduct is unwelcome and what it does to the person, not by whether the sender 'meant well' or 'was only joking'.

scenes.heading: Silence is not consent
scenes.narration: Many people don't object out loud, especially to a supervisor who controls their shifts or appraisal. Not saying no is not the same as saying yes.

scenes.heading: The phone is part of work
scenes.narration: Late-night personal messages, comments on someone's profile photo, unsolicited images or voice notes, pressure for video calls: on WhatsApp the pattern is often persistence after no reply.

scenes.heading: Small things build walls
scenes.narration: Jokes, nicknames and exclusion seem minor alone. Tolerated, they create a climate where bigger harms feel normal.

scenes.heading: Look for the pattern
scenes.narration: Ask three questions: is it unwelcome, is it about gender or sexual in nature, and is it affecting the person's work or sense of safety?

cards.title: How harm escalates
cards.caption: The top rests on the base. When the everyday layers are tolerated, the serious ones become more likely.

items.label: Assault and coercion
items.detail: Physical assault, sexual coercion: criminal matters as well as workplace ones.

items.label: Threats and 'comply or else'
items.detail: Linking shifts, confirmation or promotion to going along.

items.label: Unwanted touch and images
items.detail: Touching, sending or sharing sexual or edited images.

items.label: Persistent messages and comments
items.detail: Repeated late-night messages, remarks about looks or private life.

items.label: Jokes, stereotypes, exclusion
items.detail: Sexist 'banter', nicknames, leaving people out of groups and meetings.

cards.title: WhatsApp: red flag or professional?
cards.prompt: Sort each message pattern from Saffron Line staff phones.

items.text: 'Your DP is looking very nice today 😉' from a supervisor at 1 am
'Line 3 down, can you check the oven log?' sent at 11 pm during a night trial
Repeated 'why aren't you replying?' after no response
A forwarded edited photo of a colleague with a joke caption
A team group reminder about tomorrow's 9 am audit
Adding a colleague to a private 'fun' group without asking, then sending personal voice notes
'Thanks for covering today, appreciated' after a shift swap
Asking a junior to switch to video call 'to talk privately' about nothing work-related

cards.question: A supervisor says his messages to a trainee were 'just friendly' and he 'meant no harm'. She has not replied to most of them and has asked a colleague to swap shifts to avoid him. Which factor matters most?
options: His intention, since he says he meant no harm
Whether she ever told him 'no' in writing
Whether the messages were sent on a company phone
Whether the conduct is unwelcome and its impact on her work and safety
cards.explanation: Harassment is judged on whether conduct is unwelcome and its effect, not on stated intent. Her silence and shift swaps are signs it is unwelcome. A written 'no' is not required, and the device does not decide it.

cards.title: When someone confides in you
cards.caption: Whether you are a colleague or a manager, how you respond in the first ten minutes shapes whether they ever speak up again.

items.label: Listen without judging
items.detail: Let them speak. Don't interrupt, interrogate or ask 'why didn't you…?'.

items.label: Thank and reassure
items.detail: 'Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing.'

items.label: Be honest on confidentiality
items.detail: Promise discretion and need-to-know sharing, not total secrecy.

items.label: Explain the options
items.detail: Informal resolution, inquiry committee, ombudsperson, and other legal routes.

items.label: Ask what they need
items.detail: Safety, shift changes, leave, support. Act with their consent where possible.

items.label: Refer, record, follow up
items.detail: Refer to the committee or HR, note facts and dates, check in later. Don't investigate yourself.

cards.title: Preserving online evidence
cards.prompt: Mehwish's friend at another plant receives harassing messages. Put the evidence steps in the best order.
steps: Don't delete or reply angrily; leave the messages in place
Take screenshots showing the sender's number or name, date and time
Export or back up the chat and save copies somewhere secure
Write a short note of what happened, when, and who else saw it
Take the evidence to the inquiry committee or HR
If an online offence may be involved, consider a complaint to the cybercrime authority

cards.title: The distributor dinner
cards.setting: A restaurant on Shahrah-e-Faisal, Karachi. Saffron Line's annual distributor dinner. Bilal is visiting from the plant.

lines.text: A large distributor, Mr Shafiq, has had Sana seated next to him. His comments have drifted from targets to her appearance.
(quietly, to Bilal at the buffet) He's put his hand on my chair twice and asked if my husband 'lets me' travel. I need this account.
Then let's not leave you alone with it. Give me one minute.
(at the table) Shafiq sahib, I've been meaning to ask about your Hyderabad warehouse. Sana, would you take my seat so we can talk shop?
(later) Thank you. That was smooth. But I don't want this to happen at the next dinner either.
Agreed. I'll back you when you raise it with Hamid sahib, and the account plan can't depend on you sitting next to him.

cards.title: The five Ds of stepping in

cards.back: Name it calmly: 'That's not okay, please stop.' Best when you feel safe and it won't escalate the danger.
Interrupt the moment indirectly: a question, a spilt drink, 'Sana, the boss is calling you'. Low risk, often very effective.
Get help from someone with more authority or skill: a manager, security, HR, a committee member.
If you couldn't act in the moment, check in afterwards: 'I saw that. Are you okay? What would help?'
Note or screenshot what happened, then give it to the person affected. Never share it around or post it without their consent.

cards.title: The meme in the group
cards.situation: In the 'Karachi Sales Team' WhatsApp group (34 members, including two managers), a colleague posts a meme mocking 'lady drivers' with a photo of Hira, a new sales officer, edited onto it. Three people react with laughing emojis. Hira is in the group and goes silent. You are a peer, not a manager. What do you do?

choices.text: Ignore it; reacting will only make it a bigger deal for Hira.
choices.outcome: The meme stays up. Two more 'jokes' follow that week. Hira reads the silence as agreement and starts avoiding the team.

choices.text: Post a short, calm message ('Not funny, let's keep this group professional') and message Hira privately to check she's okay and ask what she'd like; save a screenshot for her if she wants to report it.
choices.outcome: The poster deletes the meme. One of the managers adds 'Agreed'. Hira thanks you, and decides to raise it informally with her manager with your screenshot. Direct, delay and document, used together.

choices.text: Forward the screenshot to the wider company group so everyone sees how bad the poster is.
choices.outcome: Now Hira's edited photo has been seen by 300 more people. Spreading the image harms the person you meant to help. Documenting means giving evidence to her, not broadcasting it.

choices.text: Message the poster privately to say it's not okay, but say nothing to Hira.
choices.outcome: The poster deletes it, which helps. But Hira never learns anyone noticed, and doesn't know she has support or options if it happens again.

cards.title: Retaliation: the second harm
cards.body:
**Retaliation** is any negative treatment of someone because they complained, supported a complaint or gave evidence. It can be more damaging than the original conduct, because it tells everyone what happens to people who speak up.

Watch for:
- Sudden poor ratings, missing data or 'performance concerns' after a complaint
- Being removed from groups, meetings, shifts or projects
- Rumours, cold-shouldering and 'jokes' about the complaint
- Pressure to withdraw or to 'settle it informally' for the team's sake

Managers have a duty to stop it. Treat retaliation as **serious misconduct**, keep the complainant's work assessed on evidence, and keep details on a **need-to-know** basis. Interim steps, such as changing reporting lines or shifts, should not punish the complainant: move the accused where possible, and agree any change with the complainant first.

cards.title: Allyship in action
cards.prompt: Match each ally behaviour to an example from Saffron Line.

pairs.right: 'As Mehwish said ten minutes ago, the oven downtime fix is hers. Let's give her the floor.'
Hamid puts Sana's name forward for the North role and vouches for her in the room.
Bilal takes paternity leave and leaves at 5 pm on Tuesdays for the school pick-up.
'Yaar, that comment about her husband was out of line. Let's not.'
Asking Sana what support she wants before acting, instead of 'rescuing' her.

cards.title: Performative or real allyship?
cards.caption: Allyship is measured by what changes for the other person, not by how supportive the ally looks.

items.label: Visibility
items.left: Posts on Women's Day, silent the rest of the year
items.right: Speaks up in the meeting where it matters

items.label: Credit
items.left: Repeats a woman's idea as his own
items.right: Names who had the idea first

items.label: Help
items.left: Decides what she needs and 'rescues' her
items.right: Asks what she wants and follows her lead

items.label: Care work
items.left: Praises mothers in speeches
items.right: Takes his own leave and covers fairly

cards.title: Running an inclusive meeting
cards.body:
- **Timing**: schedule key meetings in working hours, not 7 pm 'quick catch-ups'.
- **Rotate the chores**: note-taking, tea and booking rooms are not one person's job.
- **Stop interruptions**: 'Hold on, Mehwish was mid-point.'
- **Credit by name**: record who raised which idea in the minutes.
- **Bring in quiet voices**: go round the table or invite written input before the meeting.
- **Hybrid fairness**: call on remote participants first sometimes.
- **Venues**: choose places all staff can attend safely and comfortably.

cards.question: A manager tells a complainant: 'While the inquiry runs, it's better if you work from the warehouse office so things stay calm.' She did not ask for this and loses her sales territory. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing; separating the parties is always correct
The interim step punishes the complainant and may be retaliation; the accused should be moved where possible, with her agreement on any change
The manager should have moved both of them to the warehouse
The manager should have waited until the inquiry ended before doing anything
cards.explanation: Separating the parties can be right, but the complainant should not bear the cost. Moving her against her wishes and taking her territory signals punishment for complaining.

cards.title: How Bilal changed the plant
cards.body:
After admitting he stayed silent, Bilal made four changes at Sheikhupura:

1. **Groups**: work WhatsApp groups now have a pinned rule (work only, no images of colleagues) and two admins, one of them a woman.
2. **Shift briefings**: every briefing ends by naming one committee member people can approach, including a woman member.
3. **Retaliation watch**: for six months after any complaint, Bilal personally reviews the complainant's ratings and shift allocations for sudden changes.
4. **Men talking to men**: he raised the group photo at a supervisors' meeting himself: 'I saw it and said nothing. That was wrong. From now on, we say something.'

The fourth change mattered most. Coming from the plant manager, it made speaking up normal.

cards.title: Bystander Bridge crossed
items: Harassment is judged by whether conduct is unwelcome and its impact, not intent; silence is not consent.
On WhatsApp, look for persistence after no reply, comments on looks, unsolicited or edited images and pressure for private calls.
When someone confides: listen, thank, be honest about confidentiality, explain options, ask what they need, refer and follow up; don't investigate yourself.
Preserve evidence: don't delete, screenshot with sender, date and time, back up, note witnesses.
The five Ds: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document; give documentation to the person affected, never spread it.
